articles.title: The Teams That Have My Heart
articles.deck: Josh King on the teams that still have his heart—and why a Raiders upset in Denver could put Fernando Mendoza in the conversation.
articles.author: Josh King
articles.label: By Josh King
articles.body:
The only teams I’m truly a fan of are the Pittsburgh Pirates, the Las Vegas Raiders, and Pitt Panthers football and basketball.

I grew up a huge Penguins fan, but over the years I became more a fan of the league and less attached to Pittsburgh. When they tore down Mellon Arena—the Igloo—it broke the bond I’d carried with the team since childhood. PNC Park, on the other hand, still has that magic.

I was a clubhouse reporter for the Pirates for four years: 2016, 2017, 2018, and 2025. As I’ve gotten older, I’ve realized I enjoy watching games from home more than being at the ballpark.

I watch or listen to almost every Pirates game. More than anything, I want to see them win a World Series.

I do like the Steelers, but my first game in person was against the Oakland Raiders. The first time I saw the Legion of Doom and experienced Raiders fans, I knew I was hooked for life. I love going to road games, and I was there for the game that became Josh McDaniels’ last as head coach.

I’ve been a Raiders fan since they lost the Super Bowl to the Buccaneers, but the JaMarcus Russell years were when I really started watching every game. Tom Cable was the coach, and Bruce Gradkowski shocked the Steelers and the football world. You’ll still catch me watching the Steelers pretty regularly, but there’s nothing quite like a Raiders game.

Some of my biggest winning bets have come from Raiders games.

A lot of people have been asking me about Mendoza. I watched the game against Seattle, and the play calling left me scratching my head. Going into the Denver game, the Raiders are long shots to win, but I genuinely believe an upset could put Mendoza in the conversation with Ben Roethlisberger. Ben was arguably the greatest rookie quarterback we’ve ever seen, winning all 14 of his starts. I don’t think we’ll ever see anything like that again.

I’m not saying Mendoza is the next Ben Roethlisberger or the second coming of Christ. I like the kid, and a lot of people believe he’s special. If he really is, pulling off an upset in Denver could set the tone for his entire career. Raider Nation isn’t easily impressed, so that would certainly get people’s attention.

I also regularly listen to Hondo Carpenter on YouTube. Look him up if you haven’t already; he puts out some great Raiders content.

People have also been asking me about the Cousins trade. I liked it. The Raiders still could have made the playoffs, but for whatever reason, they seem to be clearly punting on those chances—unless they pull off the upset against Denver. If they do, they’ve got a legitimate shot.

The biggest problem is that this team simply doesn’t have enough wide receivers who can make plays. I’ve been screaming about that all year.

As for Coach Kubiak, he was doing a perfect job until halftime. Then he put more pressure on his team by declaring, “WE ARE GOING TO WIN THIS GAME.” Well, they didn’t. I had a lot of money riding on the Raiders and cashed out shortly after that.

Maxx Crosby continues to dominate, and I’m incredibly thankful Baltimore failed him on that physical. The Ravens could end up paying a serious price for that decision, especially if they miss the playoffs.

I also took some heat from podcast listeners because I said I wanted to see Aidan O’Connell get a few starts. Well, I got my wish. Honestly, I would have been perfectly content going into the season with him as the starter. I wanted to see where his development and progression stood.

Mendoza was sacked six times last week. No quarterback can keep taking that kind of punishment and expect to stay healthy. Just look at what happened to David Carr in Houston. You can take only so many hits before they start affecting your career.

As for Jeanty, I think he’ll be fine. The Raiders simply don’t have enough playmakers on the outside, and that’s clearly affecting their running game. Defenses don’t have to respect the passing attack enough, making life much harder for everyone in the backfield.

At the end of the day, I’m a Pirates and Raiders fan through and through. I’ll always appreciate Pittsburgh sports, but those are the teams that truly have my heart.

articles.title: The Legionaries Aren’t Going Anywhere
articles.deck: After two decades of ball hockey, championships, injuries, and setbacks, Josh King explains why the Legionaries still matter—and why he’s not walking away.
articles.author: Josh King
articles.label: By Josh King
articles.body:
If you type “Indianapolis Legionaries” into YouTube, you’ll see what might be the worst ball hockey team ever assembled in American history.

A lot of you know how much I loved the Indiana Ball Hockey Association (IBHA) at Ellenberger Park. I was suspended indefinitely this past year, and I’ve spent considerable time considering a defamation lawsuit and other claims. I haven’t filed because I genuinely don’t like being on the offensive side of karma. Still, I’m willing to defend myself. If the president wants to challenge me, I’m willing to let the courts decide who’s right.

For those new to the ball hockey drama, I’ve played this sport for more than 20 years. I’ve been suspended from every rink I’ve ever played at, largely because ball hockey is an incredibly physical sport. For guys who can’t inline or ice skate, it’s often their only opportunity to play hockey. A lot of us came from farming backgrounds, where life back home wasn’t always easy. Hockey was our escape. For many of us, it was all we had.

I originally bought the Legionaries from IBHA and took the team to Pennsylvania. We won three consecutive championships before eventually falling short of another title. We invested in players, bought some of the nicest jerseys around, and watched the franchise fall from one of the higher divisions all the way to the bottom league, where we currently sit in last place.

We might be the oldest team ever assembled. I’m actually the second-youngest guy on the roster. My ball hockey game has fallen off a cliff, and I was getting ready to call it quits. Then I realized something: Whenever I’m playing regularly, I’m in great shape. When I’m not playing, I tend to let myself go.

I want JKSPORTSBOOK to promote healthy habits, and I’ve decided I’m going to keep playing in 2027. I’m also committed to keeping the Indianapolis Legionaries alive for at least another decade.

2027 will be my final season playing in the NBHL. I’ve personally agreed to play for Jacksonville this year, and I’m looking forward to helping the expansion team find its footing.

Here’s a little-known fact: I’ve never won a game in the NBHL.

I started with Indianapolis, where I accounted for 66% of the team’s total goals despite missing half the games. I won the team’s scoring title and, naturally, self-appointed myself MVP.

Then I went to California Tier 2, where I had a goal disallowed, smoked a lot of weed, and got completely messed up on a cannabis pill—I didn’t even know those existed. I was basically benched and never returned. I even paid a third party to review my game footage. They said I played just fine, which probably wasn’t the feedback they would have preferred to give me.

After that, I played in Texas for Oklahoma, where I took a hit to the back that resulted in several broken bones. It completely ruined the experience for me. I tried working my way back, but I was never quite the same player.

Eventually, I started getting back into ball hockey shape, only to get banned from Indiana.

I took six months off to recover. This fall, I started strong, but my game eventually fell off a cliff again. I was ready to walk away from ball hockey and focus exclusively on roller and ice hockey.

Then something unexpected happened. Playing with the older guys reminded me why I fell in love with this sport in the first place. I started enjoying the game again, even while thinking I was playing my final season.

The Legionaries are on YouTube tonight, and I’ll be creating some content since I’m out of the lineup. Our final two regular-season games are Monday night, and I’m 50/50 on whether I’ll suit up.

Moving forward, I’ll share more in-depth ball hockey stories right here on this page. There’s a lot more to this story, but here’s a general synopsis of why the Legionaries mean so much to me.

1. The Scottdale Bears

I played for the Scottdale Bears for over a decade. Before joining Indianapolis, they were my favorite team of all time. That organization will always hold a special place in my heart.

2. The Original Indianapolis Experience

I was genuinely shocked by how bad the roster was when I first joined Indianapolis. Despite that, the Legionaries quickly became special to me. I met a lot of people in Indy whom I still proudly call friends today.

3. The Pennsylvania Magic

The first Legionaries team in Pennsylvania had something special. We had a certain chemistry and a little bit of magic. Some guys resented me for featuring Stu so often, but we were just having fun and enjoying the experience.

4. The NIL Experiment

When I started paying players last year, it became painfully obvious that my NIL experiment had failed. In my view, the players didn’t appreciate the investment. Ironically, the team stopped winning after I started paying them. That Legionaries roster was probably my least favorite of all time.

It was an expensive lesson, but one worth sharing.

5. The Future

The Legionaries aren’t going anywhere. I plan on playing until I’m 65, which means this franchise could be around until at least 2052.

Twenty years of ball hockey, countless teammates, championships, disappointments, suspensions, injuries, and some unbelievable stories. I’ve had my ups and downs with this sport, but I still love it.

The Legionaries will outlive most of the rosters that have worn the jersey. If I have anything to say about it, they’ll still be around long after I’m done playing. This story is far from over.

articles.title: Inside the Fed: The Beginning
articles.deck: An invitation to an Indiana Sentinels game introduced Josh King to Single-A hockey and set him on an unexpected path through the FPHL.
articles.author: Josh King
articles.label: By Josh King
articles.body:
I started my second “career” as an agent less than a year ago.

It all started when Darrin Trebes, the number one pick in Indiana ball hockey, invited me to attend an Indiana Sentinels game. The last thing I wanted to do was attend a minor league hockey game.

Growing up, I was a huge Pittsburgh Penguins fan. Mario Lemieux and Jaromir Jagr were my favorites, just like every other kid growing up in Pittsburgh. Kovalev, Lang, Straka, and Kasparaitis were also among my favorites.

Hockey was part of my childhood. Fred Traynor, who was related to my stepmother, was the first general manager of the Wheeling Nailers. I loved going to Wheeling and experiencing that atmosphere.

A few years ago, though, I returned as a member of the media, and it just didn’t hit the same.

I’d always declined invitations to see the Indy Fuel. Quite honestly, I found it boring. So when I was invited to see the Sentinels, a team playing at an even lower level, I wasn’t exactly jumping at the opportunity.

But something happened that night.

Single-A hockey hooked me almost instantly. Not necessarily because of the level of play, but because of the presentation. The atmosphere, the experience, and the entire operation opened my eyes to something I hadn’t considered before.

I immediately saw the value in it, particularly because of the lack of NHL affiliation. I couldn’t believe this level of hockey existed, and I started looking at it through an entirely different lens.

Then I had a question.

Knowing Trebes could play, I couldn’t understand why he wasn’t on a roster. Why wasn’t someone giving him an opportunity?

That one question set me down the strangest, most unexpected path of my career.

What started as an invitation to a hockey game became something much bigger.

Welcome to Inside the Fed.

I’ll take you behind the scenes, introduce you to the people, tell you the stories, and show you a side of this world that no other member of the media gets to see.

We’re going places you won’t find anywhere else.

articles.title: The VIP Life Was Brutal. The Next Chapter Is Compliance.
articles.deck: Josh King reflects on life as a casino VIP, the cost of chasing an image, and the more transparent approach he plans to take in 2027.
articles.author: Josh King
articles.label: By Josh King
articles.body:
Dear JKSportsBook fans,

A lot of you ask me what it was really like living at MGM National Harbor.

Let me tell you... IT WAS BRUTAL.

I couldn't stop eating Shake Shack and sushi every single day. It was freezing cold, and I was required to wager $1,000 per game, all while the casino was essentially hoping I'd lose.

I won the poker tournament, then proceeded to give most of those winnings back playing blackjack. When I finally walked out, I was up $7,000 but approximately 77 pounds heavier. (Okay, realistically, 40, but it FELT like 77.)

I ultimately decided to leave on my own.

Being a VIP sounds glamorous until you actually live it. The pressure, the expectations, the constant action... it can become exhausting.

I was also betting someone else's picks (Cooperinthe412), and I felt obligated to tip, pay out, and keep the whole thing moving. Looking back, it became a spiral of spending money for the sake of vanity and maintaining an image.

And that's something I want to be honest about.

I still believe in sports betting, but what I've always loved most is the media side of this business.

That's why I'm making a major change.

On January 1, 2027, I'm returning to gambling full-time, but this time with a different approach. I want to understand the tax code, learn the legitimate tax implications and potential benefits of gambling, and educate our audience along the way.

One word will define this next chapter:

COMPLIANCE.

I want everything we do to be aboveboard. That means understanding IRS requirements, keeping proper records, documenting everything, and making sure our other business endeavors are operating the right way, too.

I'm not interested in cutting corners. I'm interested in building something sustainable, transparent, and educational.

And trust me, the content is going to be AMAZING.

Between now and January 1, 2027, we'll be sharing some incredible behind-the-scenes media coverage from the past. You'll get to see a side of this industry that most people never experience.

Most importantly, I want to teach people how to fish for themselves.

If I've made mistakes along the way, I want you to learn from them. If I've experienced something firsthand, I want to share it. And if there's a better, smarter, and more responsible way to approach this business, we're going to explore it together.

This next chapter isn't just about gambling. It's about education, media, transparency, and building something bigger than ourselves.

Let's learn, grow, and fly together.

January 1, 2027. We're just getting started.

articles.title: A Letter to the FPHL: Building What Comes Next
articles.deck: The story of the Federal Prospects Hockey League and the people building a game without limits.
articles.author: Josh King
articles.label: By Josh King
articles.body:
Dear Players of the Federal Prospects Hockey League,

My name is Joshua King.

Prior to entering minor league hockey, I built my career managing successful ball and roller hockey clubs, where strong organization, top-tier branding, and robust NIL opportunities consistently attracted top talent.

When I attended my first FPHL game less than a year ago, I immediately saw untapped potential in the league. Since becoming an agent, I have built a strong roster—particularly for European players—by ensuring my clients earn top market value through comprehensive NIL programs, including upgraded housing and personal transport.

The FPHL has enormous potential as an independent league, unburdened by rigid, traditional systems. Moving forward, I am transitioning from agent work to team ownership. My goal is to build dynamic, high-energy rosters featuring players with distinct playstyles and strong individual brands.

I am hosting a segment on Inside the Fed, co-hosted by Shaun Weiss, where I will discuss these plans and the future of the league in more detail.

Best regards, Joshua King
